prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, which opened a new regime of accuracy in the measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks first after reading the other ballots. The physical idea is a single, sharp invention: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice makes the light shift of the clock transition vanish while many atoms are interrogated at once, which is what allows fractional uncertainty near 1e-18 together with very good stability. Its consequences are concrete and checked in many laboratories: relativistic geodesy at the centimetre level, tighter limits on drifting constants and on dark-matter couplings, and the evidence base for redefining the second. Ye's group carried the scheme to record accuracy and stability and developed the many-body clock, so the two-name credit follows the proposal and its decisive realisation without forcing an arbitrary cut. From my own work on atomic structure and many-body effects I can judge that controlling lattice light shifts, hyperfine mixing and blackbody shifts at this level is real physics and not just engineering refinement.
statement.case_against: The strongest counterargument is that B041 has much broader support (four first places) and that topological insulators reorganised condensed matter far more widely than clocks have reorganised metrology. A second concern is lineage: the 2005 prize (combs) and the 2012 prize (ion control) are adjacent, so some will see clocks as a continuation of precision spectroscopy and as technology refinement. There is also a real attribution gap, since Lemonde, Takamoto, Hollberg and the ion-clock groups are outside the credit, and the redefinition of the second is not yet complete.

responses.point: Topological insulators (B041) are the first choice: a new classification of band insulators with clear experimental fingerprints, mature after about two decades, with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan favoured and Mele left out.
responses.response: I agree on the scientific weight and ranked B041 third myself; spin-orbit physics is close to my field and the case is convincing. My reservation is the credit rather than the merit. Your own trio drops Mele, whose Z2 work with Kane is the core of the theory, and Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe state that Molenkamp measured. Any three-person B041 prize therefore needs a choice the evidence does not make for us. Clocks have a cleaner attribution (proposal plus decisive realisation) and a comparable fingerprint, namely a measured uncertainty orders of magnitude below the caesium standard. I would not call B041 wrong, only less ready on credit than B013.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks are important, but it is not clear the committee treats clocks as a discovery rather than a technology refinement; his first choice is the compound topological entry B029.
responses.response: I take this seriously, but I think it misdescribes the work. The magic-wavelength condition is a physical insight about differential polarisability at a chosen wavelength, not a refinement of a known design, and what followed was a measurement of nature: gravitational redshift across millimetres and tests of constants. The Wineland and Hall precedents show the committee already honours measurement science that changes what can be observed. On B029, I agree with your own caveat that it bundles quantum spin Hall and quantum anomalous Hall into one entry and leaves out Mele, so it overlaps with B041 and has the same allocation problem.

responses.point: Ranks lattice clocks second as a sharp invention of the kind the prize criteria favour, with a clean two-laureate attribution, though Ye's other work could be argued elsewhere.
responses.response: I agree with the invention framing and with the clean attribution. On Ye's other work (B007), I think it should not count against him here, since the clock contribution stands alone on atomic-clock accuracy and many-body clock physics. Where I differ from you is on B041, which you rank first. I think its merit is not in question but the three-name allocation is, as you note yourself about Mele, and I would not rank it above a candidate that needs no compromise on names.

responses.point: Ranks clocks first for the clean idea, the 1e-18 uncertainties and the coming redefinition of the second, but flags that the Katori and Ye split might look uneven given the earlier comb prize.
responses.response: I agree that the split between Katori's proposal and Ye's realisation is the point to examine. My view is that it is defensible: Katori has priority on the scheme and the first Sr demonstrations, and Ye's contribution is the accuracy and stability that made the clock a metrological instrument. The comb prize concerned the frequency ruler that makes optical clocks readable; it did not cover trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength. Where we may differ is B031. You see it as a capstone of cold-atom prizes, but I think it has a harder credit problem, since Cirac, Zoller and Jaksch proposed the Hubbard realisation and the five-name list cannot be cut to three without a theory-experiment trade.

responses.point: Ranks trapped-ion quantum computing (B026) second but notes that the 2012 prize narrows what is left and that Zoller appears on several candidates.
responses.response: I share your caution about B026. I ranked it fourth, and the 2012 prize for ion control covers much of the experimental craft, while the Cirac-Zoller proposal stands as theory that Blatt's group realised. My concern is the number of candidates built around Zoller and Cirac, which suggests the committee should settle that overlap once rather than recognise it piecemeal. I also note your caution about circuit QED (B046) being close to the 2025 prize, and I agree that makes it a weaker option this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
Whether the credit should acknowledge Lemonde, Takamoto, Hollberg and the ion-clock groups, which the exact credit list cannot hold.
Whether B041 can be given a three-name allocation that the committee considers fair without Mele, Bernevig or Zhang.
Whether Ye's separate candidacy under B007 changes how the clock credit should be framed.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B013 from the provided profile: it lists no collaboration with Katori or Ye. My documented ties are to Anne L'Huillier, the Lund attosecond group, Ursula Keller's group at ETH, Reinhold Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti and Indelicato, none of whom appear on the shortlist credits. I work in atomic theory, so I am close to the subject matter of B013, which is a field closeness and not a personal connection.
